en: The Sūtra of Vipaśyin Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court-Dispersing Grandee and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, the Subject Fǎtián, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In a past kalpa, there was a great king named Māndhātṛ, who had a crown prince named Vipaśyin. Having long resided within the deep palace, he desired to go out on an excursion and said to his charioteer, Yuga:
'Prepare the chariot and horses according to the proper rites; I wish now to go outside to tour the gardens and groves.'"
Having heard this, Yuga immediately went to the stables, prepared the carriage and horses, and brought them before the Prince.
Mounted upon it, they went outside and encountered a sick man.
The Prince said:
"Why is this person's countenance so emaciated and his physical strength so feeble? Yuga replied,
"This is a sick person."
The Prince asked,
"What is meant by 'sickness'? Yuga replied:
"The four great elements are a mere provisional combination; they are illusory and unreal. Should one even slightly deviate from maintaining their equilibrium, suffering and affliction arise;
this is what is called 'sickness. The Prince asked, "Can I avoid it?"
Yuyga replied, "All are equally illusory bodies;
the four great elements are no different, and just as when their balance is lost, one cannot escape [suffering].

Upon hearing this, the Prince’s mind was displeased; he immediately turned his carriage and returned to the royal palace, where he sat upright in contemplation of the law of illness and suffering—true and not false—and found no peace of mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When Prince Vipaśyin was strolling through the gardens for recreation,
He suddenly beheld a man afflicted by illness, His physical form haggard and withered."
He then asked the charioteer: "The Prince, too, cannot escape this;
sitting upright, he reflects upon himself that the suffering of illness is indeed no delusion.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
At that time, King Mandhātṛ asked Yuga:
"Why is it that the Prince returned from his excursion displeased? Yuga replied:
"The Prince went outside to tour the gardens and groves, where he saw a sick man whose appearance was emaciated and wretched, and his mind was ill at ease.
Not recognizing him, the Prince asked:
'Who is this person?'"
Yoga replied, "This is a sick person. He asked again:
“Can I avoid it? Yuga replied,
“Since both are equally illusory bodies composed of the four elements with no distinction between them, if their balance is lost, one cannot avoid [suffering].”
"Having heard this, the Prince immediately turned his chariot back toward the palace; he contemplated the nature of illness and therefore found no joy.
At that time, King Mandhātṛ, having heard these matters, recalled the words of the physiognomist from days past:
"If he remains at home, he will succeed to the position of an anointed Wheel-Turning Monarch; if he leaves the home life to practice with faith and devotion, he will attain the fruit of Buddhahood."

Having thought thus, he immediately provided within the palace various kinds of exquisite objects of the five desires to entertain the Prince, intending to cause him to become so attached that he would abandon his intention to leave the home life.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“King Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, knowing his son had returned from his excursion, felt neither joy in body nor mind;
he feared the youth might seek to leave the household life.”
"Then, with the most excellent pleasures— forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures—
to delight the Prince’s heart, so that he may later succeed to the royal throne.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
At that time, Prince Vipaśyin said to Yu-ga:
"Prepare the chariots and horses for me according to the proper rites; I shall now go outside the city to tour the gardens and groves."
Having heard this, Yūga immediately went to the stables, prepared the carriage and horses, and brought them before the Prince.

Mounting it, they departed the city and encountered an old man whose hair and beard were white, whose body and mind were weary and debilitated, who walked forward leaning on a staff, groaning and lacking strength.
The Prince asked, "Who is this person? Yuga replied:
"This is an old man. The Prince asked,
"What is meant by 'old'?"

Yoga replied: "The illusory body of the five aggregates undergoes the transformations of the four phases. Beginning from infancy and childhood, one is unaware as it progresses through youth and adulthood to old age; when the eyes grow dim, the ears deaf, and the body and mind decay, this is called 'old age.'"
The Prince asked,
"Shall I be spared from this? Yuga replied:
"Though noble and base differ, their illusory bodies are no different; as days pass and months come, one must likewise grow old.
Upon hearing this, the Prince was displeased and returned home, where he entered meditative concentration to contemplate the law of the suffering of old age, realizing that none can escape it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Prince Vipaśyin, suddenly beholding an old man,
Whose beard and hair were all white, Holding a staff and lacking physical strength,"
"Entering meditative concentration and reflecting with discernment, one sees that all conditioned phenomena do not abide for even a single moment; there is no one who can escape this.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
When King Mandhātṛ saw that the prince was unhappy, he asked Yuga,
"Why is my son’s heart so displeased? Yuga replied:
When the Prince went outside and saw an old man, he asked,
"What kind of person is this? Yuga replied:
"This is an old man," the Prince asked again,
"What is meant by 'old'?"

Yogā replied: "The illusory body of the five aggregates undergoes the transformations of the four phases. Beginning from infancy and childhood, one is unaware as it progresses through youth and adulthood until reaching old age; when the eyes grow dim, the ears go deaf, and the body and mind decay, this is called 'old age.'"
The Prince asked, "Am I also exempt? Yuga replied:
"Though high and low differ, their illusory bodies are no different; as days pass and months come, one must likewise grow old.

Having heard this, the Prince returned with a heavy heart; he entered meditative concentration and contemplated that there was truly no one who could escape this fate, which is why he was so displeased.
When the king heard these words, he recalled the prediction of the physiognomist from the past:
"If he remains at home, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King;
if he renounces the world, he will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood."

At that time, King Mandhātṛ, having thought thus, again sought to delight the prince with the exquisite pleasures of the five senses, intending to cause him to become so attached that he would abandon his intention to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“King Mandhātu, his father, saw his son and was not pleased at heart;
Recalling the words of the physiognomist of old, he feared the youth would seek to leave the household life.”
"By means of the five sublime sensual pleasures, they delight his mind in various ways,
just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, enjoys himself in the Nandana Grove.
When the Blessed One had spoken this verse, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
At that time, Prince Vipaśyin said to Yuga:
"Prepare my chariot and horses according to the proper rites; I wish now to go outside to tour the gardens and groves."
Having heard this, Yu-ga immediately went to the stables, prepared the carriage and horses, and brought them before the Prince.
As they rode out, he saw a great multitude of people surrounding the carriage, wailing aloud with loud cries.
The Prince asked, "Who is this person? Yuga replied:
"This is the sign of death.
The Prince asked,
"What is meant by 'death'?"

Yoga replied: "In this floating world of human life, lifespans are of varying lengths; yet once one departs from others, the breath ceases and the spirit passes away. One is forever separated from loved ones and dwells eternally in the desolate wilderness while kinsmen wail in grief—this is called death."
The Prince asked, "Can I avoid it? Yuga replied:
"The three realms offer no peace; none have escaped birth and death, and even the Prince’s own body cannot escape it.

Having heard this, the Prince became displeased in both body and mind, turned his chariot back to the palace, and entered meditative concentration to contemplate that the nature of impermanence is not to be cherished. He thought, "How may I now escape this suffering?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When Prince Vipaśyin saw that person whose life had ended, He immediately questioned his charioteer: 'None can escape this suffering.'"
Sitting alone in self-reflection, [I consider] what is true and not erroneous:
how may my own body escape the affliction of impermanence?
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
King Mandhātṛ asked Yuga, "Why does the prince not take pleasure? Yuga replied:
"The Prince went out of the city and saw a dead man.
He asked, 'Who is this person?'"
Yoga replied, "This is a sign of death. The Prince said:
“What is meant by ‘death’?

Yuga replied, “In this floating world of human life, the lifespan is either short or long; when one suddenly parts from it, the breath ceases and the spirit departs. One is forever separated from those they love and dwells eternally in the desolate wilderness. As kinsmen wail in grief, this is what is called death.”
The Prince asked, "Can I avoid this? Yuga replied:
"The three realms offer no peace; one has not yet escaped birth and death, and thus cannot be exempt from them.

Having heard this, the Prince turned his chariot back toward the palace. Entering meditative concentration, he contemplated that there was truly no one who could escape, and for this reason, he found no joy.
When the king heard these words, he recalled the prophecy of the physiognomist from days past:
"If he remains at home, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King; if he leaves the home life, he will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
"Furthermore, by means of the pleasures of the five desires, he sought to delight the Prince, intending to cause him to become attached to them and abandon his resolve for renunciation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The King of Pāṇḍuvardhana, The Prince of Vipaśyin..."
Seeing those who have reached the end of their lives, he sighed with sorrow and was not pleased;
yet the King, with supreme delights— objects such as forms, sounds, and fragrances—
sought to entertain him and cause him to become attached, so that he would abandon his intention to leave the home life.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Then, Prince Vipaśyin said to Yu-ga:
'Prepare my chariot and horses according to the dharma; I wish now to go outside to tour the gardens and groves.'"
Having heard this, Yu-ga immediately went to the stables, prepared the chariot and horses, and brought them before the Prince.
Mounting it, they went outside, where he saw a bhikṣu with his hair and beard shaven, his body clad in a kāṣāya robe.
The Prince asked, "Who is this person? Yuga replied:
"This is one who has left the household life. The Prince asked,
"What is meant by 'one who has left the household life'?"

Yoga replied: "Having realized old age, sickness, and death, I have entered the gate of liberation; practicing patience and compassion, I seek the peace and bliss of nirvana. Having forever parted from my loved ones, I vow to become a śramaṇa, known as one who has left the household life."
Having heard this, the Prince was filled with joy and approached him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
To practice the wholesome dharmas of compassion, patience, and equanimity, and to turn one's back on worldly toil to seek peace and happiness—this is something I also wish to do."
Having spoken thus, he returned to the palace, immediately gave rise to a mind of faith, practiced the way of renunciation, and assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Prince departed from the royal city, To roam and observe the various gardens.”
Suddenly seeing an old and sick person, as well as one subject to impermanence—
whose every thought-moment does not endure for long, and who constantly undergoes various kinds of suffering;
further beholding a renunciant, who has shaved off his beard and hair,
Wearing robes of dyed color, with a dignified and graceful deportment in every movement,
always practicing impartial compassion and the various wholesome dharmas of forbearance—
for these reasons, he sought to leave the household life and renounced the pleasures of the five desires.
Parents and their retinues, kingdoms, cities, and all manner of rare treasures—
having immediately assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa, they practice patience and self-subjugation,
extinguish craving and attachment, and diligently seek the bliss of liberation.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In the city of Bandhumatī, eighty thousand people saw Vipaśyin renounce the position of his father, the king, and leave the household life to shave his head and become a śramaṇa. They each thought:
'The Prince of the noble lineage has abandoned the five desires to cultivate the holy life; we too should now likewise leave the household life.'"
After those eighty thousand people had thought thus, they immediately left the household life and became śramaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Greatly Wise Ones, supreme among men, numbering eighty thousand.”
"Following Vipaśyin, I have gone forth to practice the holy life.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"At that time, after the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin had gone forth, he departed from his own royal city with those eighty thousand people and traveled through various places until he reached a village where he entered the summer retreat."
When that summer had passed, he reflected to himself:
"Why am I now wandering about like a person who is deluded and intoxicated?
Having formed this thought, his mind attained purity; he returned to his original dwelling and, during the middle watch of the night, again reflected to himself:
"What use have I now for worldly wealth and honor?
Sentient beings are attached to saṃsāra and the cycle of birth and death; this succession of the aggregates of suffering has no end.
He then reflected further:
"This suffering of old age and death—by what condition is it produced, and how does one undergo old age and death?
Entering into samādhi, he contemplated this dharma with discernment and saw that it arises from the link of birth.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"From what cause and condition does this suffering of birth arise?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the link of existence (bhava).
Again, he reflected:
"From what cause and condition does this cause of suffering arise?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discernment and saw that it arises from the link of grasping (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, he reflected:
"By what condition is this grasping, which is the cause of suffering, produced?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the link of craving.
He further reflected:
"By what conditions is this craving, the cause of suffering, produced?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the factor of sensation (*vedanā*).
He further reflected:
"By what conditions is this cause of suffering produced?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning clarity and saw that it arises from the factor of contact (sparśa).
Furthermore, he reflected:
"From what conditions does this contact, which is the cause of suffering, arise?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discernment and saw that it arises from the branch of the six sense bases.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"By what conditions is this suffering of the six sense bases produced?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the factor of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Furthermore, he reflected:
"By what condition is this suffering of name-and-form produced?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the link of consciousness.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"From what conditions does this consciousness, the cause of suffering, arise?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, he reflected:
"From what cause and condition does this suffering of conditioned existence arise?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight and saw that it arises from the link of ignorance.

Thus, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition there are the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition there is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling; with feeling as condition there is craving; with craving as condition there is clinging; with clinging as condition there is existence; with existence as condition there is birth; and with birth as condition there are old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being.
At that time, Vipaśyin Bodhisattva further reflected:
"By what means can this suffering of old age and death be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he contemplated this dharma with discerning observation: "With the cessation of birth, old age and death cease."
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this cause of suffering in birth be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight: where there is cessation, birth ceases.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this cause of suffering be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he contemplated this phenomenon with discerning observation: "With the cessation of grasping, there is the cessation of existence."
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this grasping, which is the cause of suffering, be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight: when craving ceases, grasping ceases.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this craving, the cause of suffering, be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discernment: with the cessation of sensation, craving ceases.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this cause of suffering be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight: with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
He further reflected:
"How can this contact, which is the cause of suffering, be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discernment: with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can the cause of suffering—the six sense bases—be extinguished?
Entering samādhi, he observed this dharma with discerning insight: with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this suffering caused by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he contemplated this phenomenon with discerning observation: "With the cessation of consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form ceases."
Furthermore, he reflected:
"How can this consciousness, the cause of suffering, be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he observed this phenomenon with discerning insight: with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases.
He further reflected:
"How can these formations, which are the cause of suffering, be extinguished?
Entering into samādhi, he contemplated this dharma with discernment: "With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease."

Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering does not arise.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Vipaśyin Bodhisattva, contemplating the suffering of old age and death, used wisdom to investigate its cause:
‘By what condition and by what dharma is it produced?’”

Entering meditative concentration and observing with discernment, one knows that [suffering] arises from the link of birth, continuing up to the cause of the suffering of conditioned formations; one knows that these exist because of ignorance.
One further observes: from what do they cease?
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until old age and death are exhausted; the entire mass of suffering is thereby completely eliminated.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin further contemplated form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as arising and ceasing without abiding—like illusions and transformations, devoid of reality. As wisdom-contemplation became manifest before him, karmic tendencies and afflictions were entirely non-arising; he attained great liberation and realized perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Vipaśyin Bodhisattva, further contemplating the dharmas such as the aggregates, entered that samādhi; when the vision of wisdom appeared before him,”
The habitual tendencies of delusion, suffering, and karma— All these are utterly non-arising;
like drifting tūla-cotton, They cannot abide for even a single moment.
One achieves the Bodhi of the Buddha, The auspicious fruit of Nirvāṇa.
"Like the moon, perfectly full and luminous, its light pervades the realms of the ten directions.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"At that time, when Vipaśyin was still in the stage of a causal being, he had two doubts: first, that his own self was like one who is intoxicated; second, that afflictions such as greed increased progressively. Reflecting thus upon the dharma of dependent origination, he attained great liberation."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The body of that Buddha-Tathāgata, Which is difficult to achieve, has been achieved;
Having contemplated the dharma of dependent origination, He further severed greed, hatred, and delusion."
Having reached the ultimate further shore, He has accomplished great liberation;
Like the sun atop a mountain peak, He shines universally upon all.
—From the *Vipaśyin-buddha-sūtra*, Scroll One.
The Sūtra of Vipaśyin Buddha, Volume II.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Dharma Master Fa Tian, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, in obedience to the Imperial Decree.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"At that time, after Vipaśyin Buddha had attained enlightenment, he immediately thought to himself:
'In what place should I first preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings?'"
Having contemplated and reflected thus, [he perceived that] the great capital city where King Mandhātu resided was teeming with people and that the conditions were ripe.

Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, took up his alms bowl, and proceeded on his alms round in due order until he reached the city of Mandhātu. He went to the Deer Park of Peace and Happiness (*Anala-mṛgadāva*) and stayed there for a while to rest, dwelling in sovereignty and fearlessness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Two-Legged One, the Perfectly All-Knowing, Wanders with self-mastery, bowl in hand;
Dwelling in the Deer Park, He is fearless like a lion."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Then, Vipaśyin Buddha said to the gatekeeper:
'Go to Prince Kṛkin and his minister Tiṣya; I am currently staying in the Deer Park of Anupama, and I wish to see them.'"
When the gatekeeper had heard these words, he immediately went to Prince Kṛkin and his close minister Diśālu and reported the matter in full:
"Vipaśyin Buddha has attained the path of perfect enlightenment and has gone to the Deer Park at Anupama in the city of Bandhumatī; I wish to see him."

Having heard these words, Prince Kṛṇa immediately mounted his carriage with Diśālu and departed from the city of Bandhumatī. He proceeded to the Deer Park of Anupama and approached Vipaśyin Buddha; there he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance without ever averting his eyes.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha, wishing to cause Khaṇḍa to rejoice, believe, and accept, revealed the sublime Dharma, saying: "As taught by all the Buddhas of the past,
if one practices generosity, maintains the precepts, and exerts oneself in cultivation, one can depart from the faults of desire and form and be born in the pure heavens."

At that time, having heard these words, Prince Kṛṣṇa (Kun-da) attained purity of mind, like the mind of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin. He gave rise to a mind of right understanding, a mind free from doubt, a virtuous mind, a supple mind, a vast mind, an unimpeded mind, a boundless mind, and a pure mind. Furthermore, [the Buddha] proclaimed for him the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and provided various instructions on the practice of the Dharma.

At that time, Prince Kṛṇa and Prince Tisuru attained penetration of the Four Noble Truths; they saw the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and realized the Dharma—the firm Dharma, the Dharma of reliance, the Dharma of abiding, the immovable Dharma, the non-abandoning Dharma, and the non-empty Dharma. Just as white cotton cloth is free from all dust and impurities, so too was their mind that awakened to the Dharma.
"At that time, Prince Kṛṇa and Tiśru addressed the Buddha Vipaśyin, saying:
'Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, we vow to leave the household life and receive the precepts of the Sugata.'"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Now is precisely the right time."
He immediately shaved their hair and conferred upon them the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
In this way, that Buddha manifested three kinds of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) for those two individuals, causing them to arouse diligence and advance toward the wisdom of the Buddha:
first, the manifestation of the supernormal power of transformation; second, the manifestation of the supernormal power of preaching the Dharma.
Third, he manifested the supernatural power of subduing.
Having thus manifested it, Prince Khaṇḍa and Tiśru, through their courageous diligence, attained correspondence with true wisdom in a mere moment; they exhausted all outflows and became arhats.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One Vipaśyin preached the Dharma in the Deer Park;
Khaṇḍa and Tiṣya both came together to the place where the Buddha was."
He immediately prostrated with his head and face, gazing up with single-minded devotion.
[The Buddha] revealed the gates of giving and precepts, and the dharmas of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Having heard this, he received it with deep faith and realized the absence of arising and ceasing.
Together they sought to leave the household life and immediately received the precepts of the Sugata.
Witnessing his supernormal powers, they swiftly aroused a mind of diligence;
in an instant, all their outflows were exhausted, and they attained the state of Arhatship.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Listen attentively now!

In the city of Pāṭaliputra, there were eighty thousand people who had planted roots of merit in past lives. Upon hearing that Prince Khaṇḍa and King Tiśru had left the household life with right faith, and that the Buddha had taught them the Dharma, manifested supernatural powers, and enabled them to attain the fruit of sainthood, they reflected thus:"
“There is such renunciation, such holy life, such teaching of the Dharma, and such discipline as are rare in the world and unheard of until now; we too now wish to go forth.”

Having formed this thought, eighty thousand people simultaneously abandoned their domestic ties and departed from the city of Pūrṇamā. They proceeded to the Deer Park of Peace and Bliss at the abode of Vipaśyin Buddha, where they prostrated with their heads at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and gazed up at him with palms joined, their eyes never wavering for a moment.
The Buddha taught the Dharma for them to inspire faith in their hearts, saying:

"Just as the sublime Dharma was taught by all Buddhas of the past, if a person practices generosity, maintains the precepts, and diligently cultivates spiritual practice, they will be able to leave behind the various faults of desire, form, and afflictions, and attain rebirth in the Pure Heavens."

When the eighty thousand people heard these words, their minds attained purity, becoming like the mind of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin Buddha. They gave rise to a mind of correct understanding, a mind free from doubt, a supple mind, a virtuous mind, a vast mind, an unimpeded mind, a boundless mind, and a pure mind. Furthermore, for them he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and provided various detailed explanations of the practice of the Dharma.

Those eighty thousand people had thoroughly penetrated the Four Noble Truths; they saw the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and attained the Dharma that is firm, the Dharma that is in accordance with the Dharma, the indestructible Dharma, the abiding Dharma, the immovable Dharma, the non-abandoning Dharma, and the non-empty Dharma. Just as white cotton cloth is free from all dust and impurities, so too was their mind.
Then eighty thousand people raised their voices together and said:
"Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, please accept us so that we may go forth from the household life and receive the precepts of the Sugata."
The Buddha immediately accepted them, shaved their hair, and conferred the precepts; he further manifested three supernormal powers for that assembly to inspire them to diligent effort:
first, the power of transformation; second, the power of preaching the Dharma; and third, the power of subduing.
When this had been manifested, eighty thousand people, through their courageous diligence,
before long exhausted their outflows, attained liberation of mind,
and became arhats. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Within the city of Māndhātṛ, there were eighty thousand people who,
having heard that Khaṇḍa and the others had left the household life to realize the Noble Path,
all gave rise to pure hearts and came to where the Buddha was.

Hearing the Dharma, my heart was filled with joy; I quickly gave rise to a courageous mind and, joining my palms, addressed the World-Honored One: "I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and receive and uphold the precepts."
Having shaved his hair and received the precepts, he was further shown miraculous powers;
all fetters were severed and exhausted, like the Śirīṣa grove extinguished,
where blazing flames never arise again, having attained great liberation.
"Thus, this basis of all suffering shall be extinguished and no longer exist.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"After Vipaśyin Buddha had delivered those multitudes, he departed from the Deer Park of Peace and Bliss and proceeded toward the city of Bandhumatī. The eighty thousand bhikṣus also went to the city of Bandhumatī; arriving before the World-Honored One, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side."
The Buddha then fully explained the causes and conditions for attaining the Way, causing him to become firm in his resolve.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"To do what is difficult, to do what is most difficult, To exhaust the cycle of saṃsāra."
Thus, these eighty thousand beings, having forever severed all fetters and bonds,
were like the Emperor Sūru and the Ṛṣi Prince Khaṇḍa;
through their diligent pursuit of renunciation, they all attained the fruit of liberation.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha had this thought: 'This great assembly of bhikṣus resides in the city of Pūrṇamadra;

it is fitting that their number be reduced. Let sixty-two thousand bhikṣus go forth to various directions to wander through villages and practice as they please. After six years have passed, they shall return to the city of Pūrṇamadra and receive and uphold the Prātimokṣa.'"
While he was reflecting thus, a deva in the sky, knowing the Buddha’s thought, addressed Vipaśyin Buddha, saying: "Excellent!"

"If you allow sixty-two thousand bhikṣus to travel through various villages to practice as they wish, and after six years they return to their own country to uphold the Prātimokṣa, now is precisely the right time."
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:

"Among you bhikṣus, let sixty-two thousand people travel through various villages to practice as they wish; after six years have passed, return to your native land and receive and uphold the Prātimokṣa."
When the sixty-two thousand people heard these words, they departed from the city of Pūrṇamadra and traveled to dwell in various directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Taintless and unequaled, The Great Man, the Tamer of Men.”
Guiding the multitude of living beings, he leads them to the path of ultimate tranquility.
Now he dispatches a community of bhikṣus— the supreme disciples of the Buddha—
sixty-two thousand in number, from that city of Pūrṇamata.
"Traveling through various villages, Like a dragon of great majesty,
Practicing according to his own will, After six years, he returned to his native land.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
Those sixty-two thousand people immediately left the city and went to various villages to practice as they pleased.
In this manner, after one year and two years had passed, reaching the sixth year, those bhikṣus said to one another:
"The six years are now complete; we should return to our native land."
When he had spoken these words, a deva in the sky further addressed him, saying:
"Now is the very time; return to the city of Pūrṇamadra and receive and uphold the Prātimokṣa."
"Then, sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, by means of their own supernormal powers and the majestic virtue of the devas, reached the city of Pūrṇamā in a mere moment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The great bhikṣus of that Buddha, The assembly of sixty-two thousand."
Wandering through various villages, he fulfilled his vow for six years at will.
Thinking to himself that he wished to return, the devas and humans all gave him notice,
directing him to go back to Pūrṇavardhana City to receive and uphold the pure and cooling precepts.
Hearing this, he was filled with great joy; the hairs on his body all stood erect.
He immediately exercised his supernormal powers, traveling like one riding a great dragon-elephant, returning to his native city in an instant, moving with sovereign ease and without obstruction.
The Unsurpassed Honored One among bipeds, having appeared in this world,
has excellently taught the various codes of discipline to deliver all classes of beings;
now I shall expound for you the Prātimokṣa.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Those sixty-two thousand people reached the city of Pūrṇamadra; they went before the Buddha Vipaśyin, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side."
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now expound the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
“Patience is supreme; through patience one attains nirvāṇa.
This was taught by the Buddhas of the past: having gone forth as a śramaṇa, one should distance oneself from killing and the seven transgressions of body and speech.”
By maintaining these precepts in their entirety, one gives rise to great wisdom and attains the Buddha’s pure body, unsurpassed in the world.
One produces untainted knowledge and brings an end to the suffering of birth and death.

"At that time, as the World-Honored One was preaching this precept, there were further devas and sons of gods who, by means of their celestial power, descended from their celestial palaces to the presence of Vipaśyin Buddha. They prostrated themselves, joined their palms, and listened to and received the Prātimokṣa."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Taintless and inconceivable, Destroying darkness and reaching the further shore,
Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas Together listen to the precepts of the Great Sage.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Once, while I was staying in a pure chamber by the Seven-Leaf Rock in the city of Rājagṛha, I suddenly reflected:

'When the past Buddha Vipaśyin taught the Vinaya Piṭaka, I feared there might be devas who did not come to listen to and receive the Great Sage’s precepts; I shall now go to the devas to inquire of the Brahma hosts.'"

Having formed this thought, at that time I entered into samādhi and reached the Suyāma Heaven in the interval of a strong man extending his arm. That son of heaven bowed his head at my feet and spoke these words: "Excellent!"
“World-Honored One! It has been a long time since I last came here.

I am a śrāvaka disciple of the Buddha Vipaśyin, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One. That Buddha’s clan was Kṣatriya; he left home out of faith and belonged to the Kauṇḍinya lineage. His lifespan was eighty thousand years; his father’s name was King Māndhātṛ, and his mother’s name was Queen Māndhātṛ.”
Prince Kṣaṇḍaka and Tiśyaru renounced the world, received the precepts, and became arhats.

The foremost attendant, the Great Sage, was named Aśoka; he preached the Dharma at three assemblies, extensively delivering śrāvakas. At the first assembly, sixty-two thousand people attained arhatship; at the second assembly, one hundred thousand attained arhatship; and at the third assembly, eighty thousand attained arhatship.

Vipaśyin Buddha possessed such supreme excellence: he renounced the world in this manner, realized enlightenment in this manner, and taught the Dharma in this manner; he disciplined his disciples in this manner, causing them to don robes and carry alms bowls, to cultivate the various holy practices (*brahmacarya*), to remain far removed from the five desires, to sever the afflictions and attain liberation, to realize the dharma of non-arising, and to become *anāgāmins*.

Furthermore, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha likewise taught the Dharma to discipline beings; they donned robes and carried alms bowls, cultivated all pure conducts, distanced themselves from the five desires, severed the afflictions, realized the dharma of non-arising, and became Anāgāmins—all in this same manner.

At that time, the World-Honored One was respectfully surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras as he proceeded to the Sudarśana Heaven. When the devas of that heaven saw the Buddha, they bowed their heads at his feet in prostration; then, accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras and respectfully surrounded by them, he proceeded to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

At that time, the Heavenly King, seeing the World-Honored One from afar, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to pay homage at the World-Honored One’s feet, and spoke these words: “Excellent, World-Honored One!”
It has been a long time since I last came here.

I am a śrāvaka disciple of the Buddha Vipaśyin, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One. That Buddha’s clan was Kṣatriya, his lineage Kauṇḍinya; his lifespan was eighty thousand years. His father was named King Māndhātṛ, and his mother was named Queen Māndhātṛ; the city was also named Māndhātṛ. Prince Kṛkin and Prince Tiṣya went forth from home, received the precepts, and attained arhatship.

The Great Sage’s foremost attendant was named Aśoka; through three assemblies of preaching the Dharma, he extensively delivered śrāvakas. In the first assembly, sixty-two thousand people were delivered and attained arhatship; in the second assembly, one hundred thousand people were delivered and attained arhatship; and in the third assembly, eighty thousand people were delivered and attained arhatship.

Vipaśyin Buddha possessed such supreme excellence, such renunciation, such holy life, such realization of awakening, such teaching of the Dharma, and such discipline, that he caused his disciples to don robes, carry alms bowls, and practice the holy life; they remained far removed from the five desires, severed the afflictions, realized the dharma of non-arising, and became non-returners (anāgāmin).

Furthermore, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha likewise donned their robes and carried their alms bowls; they taught the Dharma and disciplined beings, cultivated the various holy practices, distanced themselves from the five desires, realized the dharma of non-arising, and attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
"Now the Great Muni likewise teaches the Dharma and the holy life to discipline sentient beings.
At that time, the devaputra spoke in verse:
"The Unsurpassed Honored One among bipeds Has entered into samādhi;”
Exercising swift and great supernormal powers, he departed from that Jambudvīpa realm and arrived at the Sudarśana Heaven;
just as a man of great strength swiftly extends his arms, he reached this place in a single kṣaṇa.
The World-Honored One is most rare and extraordinary;
Untainted and without obstruction, his body is pure liberation.
Like a lotus that is not wetted by water, Within hundreds of thousands of worlds, None is equal to the Buddha.
Having subdued the Great Māra, as a river sweeps away fine grass,
The various devas, such as Subhūti and others, all came together to prostrate with their heads at his feet.
They take refuge in the Most Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One of great compassion.
Taming all sentient beings, With the six sense faculties completely purified,
Giving birth to unsurpassed wisdom, One practices with diligence according to the Dharma.
In the past was Vipaśyin, The Honored One, the Truly Perfectly Awakened One.
The subtle and wondrous Dharma you have proclaimed, through three assemblies, has delivered the śrāvakas;
in their discipline and holy life, they are guarded without flaw or transgression,
pure and complete, like the moon on the fifteenth night.
The World-Honored One Śikhin, the Tathāgata Viśvabhū,
Krakucchanda of the Bhadrakalpa, Kanakamuni, and that Buddha Kāśyapa— such as these Tathāgatas.
The assembly of śrāvakas he has delivered have all attained the exhaustion of outflows;
they are no longer subject to afflictions.
Having practiced the Eightfold Noble Path and the like, they are able to remain free from the faults of the five desires.
Having attained great wisdom, he is known by all;
like Vaiśravaṇa, he constantly partakes of the flavor of nectar;
like a king who has received consecration, he forever destroys all darkness.
Just as the sun radiates its brilliant light, so too do each of the Buddha-Bhagavāns—
through their majestic deportment and their practice of the Dharma— benefit all sentient beings;
though they employ various skillful means, their guidance is without distinction.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I went to that heaven and, having heard this matter, I know that all the devas and humans, as well as those from the dharma assemblies of all Buddhas, have come to join in their sympathetic joy."

If there should be another person who delights in receiving and upholding [this teaching], whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, and who contemplates and recites it, they will be free from all delusions, forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, and attain liberation and peace.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, everyone was greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
*The Sutra of Vipaśyin Buddha*, Scroll Lower.
